prompt: You run `git merge feature/x` while on `main`. What does this do to the commit graph, assuming there is no conflict?
choices: It creates a new commit with two parents, joining the tip of main and the tip of feature/x, and leaves all existing commit hashes unchanged
It rewrites every commit on feature/x with a new hash and places them directly after the tip of main
It deletes feature/x and copies its file contents into main as a single new commit
It does nothing until you also run git commit --merge

prompt: You're on feature/x, which branched from main three commits ago. You run `git rebase main`. What happens to commits D, E, F (your feature/x commits)?
choices: They are replayed on top of the current tip of main as new commits (D', E', F') with new hashes; feature/x now points at F'
They are merged into main using a single merge commit, and their original hashes are preserved
They are deleted, and main's changes are copied into feature/x instead
Nothing changes until you also run git merge --continue

prompt: What is the core reason you should not rebase a branch that other people have already pulled a copy of?
choices: Rebase gives those commits new hashes, so your rebased branch and their existing copy no longer share history, causing duplicated commits when reconciled
Rebase permanently deletes the affected files from the remote repository
Rebase requires admin permissions that most collaborators don't have
Rebase only works on branches with zero commits ahead of main

prompt:
Mid-merge-conflict, a file contains:

<<<<<<< HEAD
port = 8080
=======
port = 3000
>>>>>>> feature/ports

You are currently on the main branch. Which value does `port = 8080` represent?
choices: main's current value (the branch you have checked out, i.e. HEAD)
feature/ports' value
The value from the most recent common ancestor commit
An automatically merged average of both branches

prompt: After manually editing a conflicted file to resolve the conflict, what is the correct next step before running `git commit`?
choices: git add <the resolved file>
git merge --abort
git rebase --continue
Nothing — git commit alone will detect the resolution automatically

prompt: A PR reviewer writes a comment prefixed with "nit:". What is this conventionally signaling to the author?
choices: This is a minor, non-blocking suggestion the author can address or skip without holding up the merge
This issue must be fixed before the PR can be approved
The reviewer is requesting the entire PR be closed
The comment applies to a different PR and was posted by mistake

prompt: A commit message ends with the line "Refs #88". What happens to issue #88 when this commit merges into the default branch?
choices: Nothing — the issue stays open; the commit is just linked to it for traceability
Issue #88 is automatically closed
Issue #88 is automatically reassigned to the commit author
A new issue is automatically created as a duplicate of #88

prompt: You're about to open a PR and want to incorporate teammates' recent changes to main into your feature branch first, keeping history linear with no merge commit. What should you run?
choices: git checkout feature/x, then git rebase main
git checkout main, then git merge feature/x
git push --force origin main
git commit --amend main
